projects.name: voicequal
projects.tagline: Audio-quality library on PyPI - published with its full 200-clip benchmark, not a favourable subset.
projects.problem: Answers the question every voice app eventually has to answer: "is this recording clean enough to process?"
projects.architecture: The system processes audio by first loading/resampling it (io.py), then extracting frame-level acoustic metrics (metrics.py). A RollingStats component (state.py) maintains historical data for calculating temporal variance and background noise levels. The assessment.py module applies a decision logic, primarily HNR-gated, to assign an audio quality tier (excellent, good, fair, poor) based on these metrics. There are two main processing paths: pipeline.py for batch file analysis and live.py for real-time streaming with added tier-stability hysteresis. Calibration (calibration.py) adjusts for microphone differences, and a command-line interface (cli.py) provides user interaction.
features: Real-time audio quality assessment
Analyzes audio using acoustic metrics, led by harmonic-to-noise ratio (HNR)
Returns a quality tier (excellent, good, fair, poor) and underlying metrics
Pure numpy/scipy, CPU-only, no models to download
Supports analysis of audio files via command-line interface or Python API
Supports real-time streaming from microphones via command-line interface or Python API
Includes microphone auto-calibration to adjust for different hardware
Streaming features a hysteresis buffer for stable tier reporting
Benchmarked against a reproducible test set for accuracy metrics
tradeoffs: Calibrated for voice/recording quality: Focuses on whether a recording is 'clean enough to process', not subjective human audio preference.
Not a certified acoustic dB meter: Background dBA is an estimate using rough dB conversion, not conforming to IEC 61672 A-weighted filter standards.
Thresholds tuned on specific test set: The decision thresholds for quality tiers were specifically tuned on the provided 200-clip benchmark set, and performance may vary on other real-world speech.
Difficulty separating 10 dB vs 5 dB mixes: The HNR metric compresses at low SNRs, making it challenging to perfectly distinguish between moderate and very loud noise conditions.
Assumes reasonable audio input: The system does not include built-in echo cancellation or noise suppression; detection accuracy can be affected by OS-level audio preprocessing.
Different mics deliver different signal levels: Requires per-mic calibration using 'voicequal listen --calibrate' for accurate background dBA readings with new hardware.
projects.demonstrates: The project demonstrates real-time audio processing techniques, including frame-based analysis and streaming. It showcases Digital Signal Processing (DSP) concepts through the calculation of various acoustic metrics (HNR, SNR, spectral flatness, concentration) using NumPy and SciPy. It illustrates the implementation of a rule-based classification system for categorizing audio quality into discrete tiers. The project also provides examples of stateful processing with rolling statistics for temporal metrics, best practices for benchmarking and evaluating DSP algorithms against reproducible test sets, and development of a user-friendly command-line interface (CLI).

projects.name: jiya-persona
projects.tagline: This site. A RAG-grounded AI rep with voice, chat, real calendar booking, and an LLM-judge eval harness.
projects.problem: The project addresses the challenge of creating an interactive, verifiable, and comprehensive professional portfolio. It provides an AI agent that can answer specific, grounded questions about a candidate's background and projects without hallucination, and facilitates practical actions such as scheduling interviews.
projects.architecture: The application follows a full-stack architecture with a Next.js 14 frontend deployed on Vercel and a FastAPI backend deployed on Render. The backend is responsible for RAG processing, LLM interactions using Google Gemini API, and integration with external services like Cal.com. For voice interactions, Vapi acts as an orchestrator for STT/TTS and communicates with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint on the backend. The RAG corpus, including ChromaDB, GitHub repo cards, and resume PDF, is baked into the backend's Docker image for deployment. Retrieval for RAG occurs before LLM calls, injecting relevant context directly into the user turn.
features: Animated portfolio displaying hero metrics, experience, and projects.
Live GitHub commit stream fetched at request time.
AI representative (chatbot and voice assistant) providing answers grounded in resume and GitHub repo specifics.
End-to-end meeting booking via Cal.com integration.
Source citation for factual claims, with refusal to fabricate information.
Voice assistant integration through Vapi, optimized for low first-token latency.
Automated generation of project cards from GitHub repository data.
Nightly GitHub Action to refresh the RAG corpus, keeping AI knowledge current.
Evaluation report demonstrating AI performance metrics (groundedness, relevance, honesty, latency).
tradeoffs: Documented 20% hallucination rate (groundedness < 0.8) primarily caused by cross-repo factual leakage, where details from one repository inadvertently appear in the context of another.
Voice mode's use of `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` optimizes for speed, which might involve a trade-off in context depth or groundedness compared to the `gemini-2.5-flash` model used for chat.
A `MAX_TOOL_TURNS` cap (4 turns) is implemented in the chat agent to prevent infinite tool-calling loops.
The heuristic-based `_detect_filter` for RAG source selection may not always perfectly infer user intent, potentially affecting retrieval relevance.

Specific common terms like 'SingoneSong' are explicitly filtered from repo name signals to prevent collisions with employer mentions, requiring more explicit cues for GitHub-related queries when these terms are present.
projects.demonstrates: This repository demonstrates the development of an advanced AI-powered portfolio application, integrating sophisticated RAG techniques across multiple data sources (PDF, GitHub repos), LLM function calling for real-world interactions (Cal.com booking), and robust voice AI integration. It showcases full-stack development using FastAPI and Next.js, cloud deployment strategies with Render and Vercel, CI/CD automation, performance optimization (e.g., latency reduction through model splitting and pre-retrieval RAG), and structured evaluation of AI agent performance.

projects.name: KV-Cache
projects.tagline: Distributed key-value cache - hash-modulo sharding, synchronous primary-replica replication, bounded LRU; 11,820 req/s on AWS.
projects.problem: Provides fast, temporary storage for key-value data, addressing the need for quick data retrieval and reducing load on primary data stores. It incorporates cache management features like time-based expiration and least-recently-used eviction to efficiently manage memory and data freshness.
projects.architecture:
The system is a KV-Cache Server with a modular architecture:
    *   Network Layer (`src/network/tcp_server.py`): Uses `asyncio.start_server()` for non-blocking I/O, handling multiple concurrent client TCP connections on port 7171.
    *   Protocol Layer (`src/protocol/`): Consists of `commands.py` (defining PUT, GET, DELETE, EXISTS) and `parser.py` (parsing raw text commands and formatting responses).
    *   Cache Layer (`src/cache/`): Implements `store.py` for core key-value storage (`KVStore`). `KVStore` itself provides in-memory storage using Python's `OrderedDict`, and integrates both Time-To-Live (TTL) for key expiration and Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction policies. The module `eviction.py` offers a standalone LRU implementation.
    *   Cluster Components (`src/cluster/`): Includes `config.py`, `replication.py`, and `router.py` for supporting cluster mode, enabling key sharding to primary nodes and replicating write operations to replica nodes. `docker-compose.yml` configures 3 nodes for a clustered deployment.
    *   Data flow: Client Request -> TCP Socket -> Protocol Parser -> KV Store (with TTL/LRU) -> Protocol Formatter -> TCP Socket -> Server Response. In cluster mode, requests may be forwarded to primary nodes or replicated to replicas.
features: High-performance in-memory key-value storage.
Asynchronous TCP server for handling concurrent clients.
Custom, simple text-based protocol with commands like PUT, GET, DELETE, EXISTS.
Time-To-Live (TTL) for automatic key expiration directly within the KVStore.
Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction policy directly within the KVStore, using `OrderedDict`.
Cluster mode support with sharding (key distribution) and replication (write mirroring) across multiple nodes.
Dockerized deployment for easy setup and scaling.
Provides development tools: an interactive client script, a load testing tool, and a benchmark script for internal performance measurement.
Configurable via command-line arguments and environment variables.
tradeoffs: No Data Persistence: Being an "in-memory" store, all data is lost upon server restart as there is no evident disk-based persistence mechanism.
Custom Protocol Lock-in: Requires custom clients to interact with the server; it is not compatible with standard key-value store protocols (e.g., Redis protocol).
Limited Data Types: Values are stored as strings (`value: str`), not natively supporting richer data structures beyond basic key-value pairs.

Scalability Complexity: While sharding and replication are implemented, managing a large-scale cluster (e.g., handling node failures, rebalancing shards) might require more advanced features not fully detailed or robust in the provided files.

Single-threaded Python Execution (GIL): Despite `asyncio` for I/O concurrency, CPU-bound operations within command execution are still limited by Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), potentially limiting peak throughput on multi-core machines for purely computational tasks (though caching is often I/O bound).
projects.demonstrates: Asynchronous programming in Python using `asyncio` for high-concurrency network services; implementation of a custom network protocol over raw TCP sockets; design and implementation of core caching mechanisms, including TTL and LRU eviction policies; modular software design principles for building a server application; basic distributed system concepts like sharding and replication; developing robust testing strategies (unit, integration, load tests); containerization with Docker and multi-container orchestration with `docker-compose`; scripting for development tasks (client, benchmark, load test, validation); and deployment considerations for cloud environments (AWS EC2).

projects.name: Distributed-Live-Polling-System
projects.tagline: Implements the backend for a live polling system featuring real-time voting, persistence, caching, and sharding.
projects.problem: The system addresses the challenge of building a scalable and resilient live polling application by implementing data persistence, application-layer caching, write batching, and sharded data distribution across multiple Redis instances using consistent hashing.
projects.architecture: The system uses a FastAPI application as its API layer, handling voting and result requests. It integrates with two Redis instances, configured via Docker Compose, to store polling data. A custom consistent hashing algorithm is implemented to distribute poll IDs across these Redis nodes. The application employs an in-memory cache for results and a background worker for batch processing of votes, flushing them to Redis periodically.
features: API endpoints for casting votes (`POST /vote`) and retrieving real-time poll results (`GET /results`).
Persistence of vote data using Redis.
Application-layer read-through caching with a 5-second TTL to reduce Redis load.
Write-behind batch processing of votes, accumulating them in memory and flushing to Redis every 10 seconds.
Distributed storage of poll data across two Redis instances using a custom consistent hashing implementation for sharding.
Health check endpoint.
tradeoffs: The system simulates a Redis cluster using two independent Redis instances with client-side sharding, which is not a true Redis Cluster and might have different operational characteristics.
In-memory caching and batching buffers (class-level dictionaries) mean that pending votes or recent cache entries could be lost upon application crashes or restarts before being flushed to Redis.

The current `ConsistentHash` implementation (as per provided code) focuses on distribution but lacks explicit handling for dynamic node additions/removals and rebalancing, which are typical concerns in production consistent hashing setups.

The `flush_batch` background task runs indefinitely with a fixed interval, requiring robust error handling for Redis operations to prevent failures from stopping the batching process entirely (not explicitly shown in provided snippets).
projects.demonstrates: Demonstrates the implementation of core concepts for building scalable backend services, including API design with FastAPI, data persistence with Redis, performance optimization through application-layer caching and write batching, and distributed system patterns like client-side sharding with consistent hashing.

projects.name: search-listings
projects.tagline: An interactive web application for smart product search combining AI embeddings and fuzzy matching.
projects.problem: Enables users to search a list of products more effectively than simple keyword search by leveraging semantic understanding and tolerance for typos/variations, providing a ranked list of relevant results.
projects.architecture: The application is a single-page Streamlit web application. It loads a pre-trained `SentenceTransformer` model and product names from a CSV file. It then creates an in-memory FAISS index from the embeddings of these product names. When a user submits a query, the query is preprocessed, embedded, and used to perform a k-nearest neighbor search on the FAISS index. The results from FAISS are then further refined and re-ranked using fuzzy matching (`fuzzywuzzy`), and custom boosts for substring and "starts with" matches, all combined with a weighted average. The top results are displayed to the user. Critical components like the model, product data, and FAISS index are cached to improve performance.
features: Interactive web-based product search interface.
Semantic search capability using sentence embeddings.
Fuzzy string matching for typo tolerance and variations.
Hybrid scoring system combining semantic similarity, fuzzy match scores, and positional boosts.
Query preprocessing to remove stop words.
Caching of model, product data, and FAISS index for efficiency.
Displays search results with match percentages.
tradeoffs: The product data and FAISS index are loaded entirely into memory, which may limit scalability for very large datasets without external storage or a more distributed FAISS setup.
The stop-word list for query preprocessing is hardcoded and relatively small.
Scoring weights for different matching components (AI, fuzzy, boosts) are hardcoded and may require tuning for optimal performance on different datasets.
Uses `encoding='latin1'` for CSV, which might not handle all character sets universally.
projects.demonstrates: How to build an interactive data application using Streamlit; implementation of a hybrid search system combining semantic similarity (embeddings) and lexical matching (fuzzywuzzy); utilizing `sentence-transformers` for creating text embeddings; working with `FAISS` for efficient similarity search on vector embeddings; techniques for caching computationally expensive operations in Streamlit applications; basic data loading, preprocessing, and manipulation with `pandas` and `numpy`.

projects.name: agentic-workflow
projects.tagline: An n8n workflow that analyzes job descriptions and resumes to provide a fit score, skill gap analysis, and personalized application advice using AI.
projects.problem: Job seekers waste time applying to mismatched roles. This workflow solves this by taking a job description and resume, extracting skills using AI, scoring the match deterministically, and producing a personalized gap analysis or application advice.
projects.architecture: The workflow is triggered by a public web form collecting job description and resume text. It then uses Google Gemini 2.5 Flash to extract skills from both inputs. A deterministic JavaScript code node compares the extracted skills to calculate a match score and identify missing skills. Based on a predefined score threshold, an IF node routes the workflow to one of two paths: a 'strong fit' path for tailored application advice or a 'weak fit' path for a skill gap analysis, both generated by Google Gemini 2.5 Flash using different personas. Finally, the structured report, including score, matched skills, missing skills, and personalized advice, is returned to the user.
features: AI-powered skill extraction from job descriptions and resumes
Deterministic match scoring and skill gap identification
Personalized application advice or upskilling roadmap based on fit score
Web form as a public user interface and trigger
Structured JSON output from AI models for reliable downstream processing
Conditional branching logic based on match score
Dynamic AI persona switching (skill extractor, application coach, gap analyst)
Workflow exposed as a callable tool via n8n Form Trigger
tradeoffs: Reliance on the quality and consistency of the AI model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) for accurate skill extraction and relevant advice generation, which may still involve potential for hallucination or misinterpretation.
The skill scoring mechanism in the JavaScript node is based on basic string matching (includes operator) which might not capture semantic similarity or skill hierarchy effectively.
The generated '30-day learning plan' for weak fits is general AI-generated advice, not a deeply personalized curriculum based on real-time learning resources or a comprehensive user profile.
The solution's scalability and performance would be dependent on the n8n instance and Google Gemini API rate limits.
projects.demonstrates: This repository demonstrates building an agentic AI workflow using a low-code orchestration platform (n8n). It highlights the effective combination of AI (LLMs) for ambiguous tasks like extraction and generation, with deterministic code for critical, reproducible logic like scoring and routing. It also showcases prompt engineering techniques for structured outputs, persona-based AI interactions, conditional workflow execution, and exposing a complex process as a user-friendly tool.

projects.name: singing_detection
projects.tagline: Production-ready AI system for detecting singing segments in audio files.
projects.problem: The system solves the problem of automatically identifying and segmenting periods of singing activity within an audio file.
projects.architecture: The system is implemented as a Python class `SingingVocalDetector`. It initializes by loading a `pyannote.audio` Voice Activity Detection (VAD) pipeline, with optional Hugging Face authentication. The core detection process involves segmenting input audio into overlapping frames, calculating RMS energy for initial silence filtering, and then processing the (concatenated) waveform through the `pyannote.audio` VAD pipeline. Frame-level singing probabilities are then enhanced using `librosa` to extract acoustic features like zero-crossing rate, RMS energy, and spectral centroid. Finally, consecutive frames exceeding a singing confidence threshold are merged into coherent singing segments. The system appears designed for command-line execution, processing one audio file at a time.
features: Detects and segments singing passages within audio files.
Utilizes a pre-trained Voice Activity Detection (VAD) model from `pyannote.audio`.
Enhances singing detection confidence through additional acoustic feature analysis (zero-crossing rate, RMS energy, spectral centroid) using `librosa`.
Offers configurable parameters for detection sensitivity (e.g., frame duration, RMS threshold, singing confidence, minimum segment duration).
Supports various audio input formats (WAV, MP3, FLAC, M4A, OGG, AAC) compatible with `librosa`.
Outputs detected singing segments in either JSON or CSV format.
Integrates with Hugging Face for model access and authentication.
Provides logging for execution status and debugging.
tradeoffs: The system's core functionality relies on external pre-trained models (specifically `pyannote/segmentation`), which requires Hugging Face authentication and an internet connection for initial model download.
Processing large audio files may lead to memory issues due to the concatenation of audio frames for VAD processing, as indicated in the `Readme.md` troubleshooting section.
The custom acoustic feature enhancement applies fixed weighting factors, which might limit generalizability or optimal performance across highly diverse audio datasets or singing styles.
Effective performance requires manual tuning of parameters like singing confidence and minimum segment duration, as suggested in the `Readme.md`.

The `models/Cnn14_16k_mAP=0.438.pth` and `models/class_labels_indices.csv` files are present in the repository but are not loaded or used by the provided `singing_detector.py` code, indicating either an incomplete implementation or unused artifacts.
projects.demonstrates: This project demonstrates the practical application and integration of advanced machine learning libraries (`pyannote.audio`, `torch`) with audio signal processing tools (`librosa`) to build a specialized audio analysis system. It showcases robust Python development practices, including object-oriented design, parameter validation, error handling, structured logging, and interaction with external model providers like Hugging Face. It provides insights into techniques for voice activity detection, acoustic feature extraction, and post-processing for segmenting specific events in audio.

projects.name: devops-ci-cd
projects.tagline: A complete CI/CD pipeline with Kubernetes deployment using GitHub Actions.
projects.problem: This project demonstrates a production-style CI/CD pipeline that automates the building, testing, security scanning, containerization, and deployment of a Java Spring Boot application to a Kubernetes cluster on AWS EC2.
projects.architecture: The project features a Java Spring Boot application. A comprehensive CI/CD pipeline is implemented using GitHub Actions. The CI workflow builds the application, runs unit tests, performs code style checks (Checkstyle), and conducts security scans (SAST with CodeQL, SCA with OWASP Dependency Check). It then builds a multi-stage Docker image, scans it with Trivy, tests the running container, and pushes the verified image to Docker Hub. The CD workflow, triggered upon successful CI, utilizes Terraform to provision an AWS EC2 instance and a security group. This EC2 instance is configured via user_data scripts to install k3s (lightweight Kubernetes) and deploy the Dockerized application as a Kubernetes Deployment, exposed via a NodePort service. The CD pipeline further logs into the EC2 to perform additional deployment steps via kubectl.
features: Automated CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions
Java Spring Boot application build and testing (Maven, JUnit)
Code quality enforcement with Checkstyle
Source code static analysis (SAST) with CodeQL
Dependency vulnerability scanning (SCA) with OWASP Dependency Check
Docker image building (multi-stage) and vulnerability scanning with Trivy
Automated Docker image push to Docker Hub
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform for AWS EC2 and Security Group provisioning
Deployment to a Kubernetes cluster (k3s) on an AWS EC2 instance
Kubernetes Deployment with liveness and readiness probes
Application exposure via Kubernetes NodePort service
Container runtime tests within CI pipeline
Integrated DevSecOps practices with security scans at multiple stages
tradeoffs: The Terraform setup provisions a single AWS EC2 instance for Kubernetes (k3s), which is not suitable for high availability or production-grade clusters.

The Kubernetes service is exposed via NodePort, opening a wide range of ports (30000-32767) in the security group and making the application directly accessible on the EC2 IP, which may not be ideal for production environments (e.g., lacking a load balancer or Ingress controller).
The AWS security group allows broad ingress from `0.0.0.0/0` for SSH, HTTP, application ports (8080), k3s API (6443), and NodePort range, which is overly permissive for a production environment.

There is an inconsistency in the specified replica count: the `README.md` and the `user_data` script in `terraform/main.tf` state 2 replicas, but the `cd.yml` workflow explicitly deploys 1 replica during the 'Deploy Application' step via `kubectl create deployment --replicas=1`.

The `cd.yml` pipeline's 'Install k3s on EC2' step re-executes `curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -`, potentially redundant or conflicting with the k3s installation from the Terraform user_data script.
The `dependency-check-suppression.xml` file is present but empty, indicating no dependency vulnerabilities are suppressed.
projects.demonstrates: This project demonstrates the complete lifecycle of a cloud-native application using modern DevOps and DevSecOps practices. It showcases how to: implement continuous integration (CI) with automated builds, tests, and static/dependency/container security scans; perform continuous delivery/deployment (CD) by provisioning cloud infrastructure (AWS EC2) with Terraform, deploying a containerized application to Kubernetes (k3s), and automating the entire process using GitHub Actions. It also highlights best practices for Dockerization and Kubernetes deployment configurations.

projects.name: SingoneSong
projects.tagline: This project implements a FastAPI-based audio analysis service that uploads audio files, extracts relevant features, performs similarity search, and supports mood-based natural language search.
projects.problem: It addresses the need for quick retrieval and mood-based search within music or audio datasets by providing a REST API to analyze, store, and search audio files based on their acoustic features and metadata.
projects.architecture: The project is a REST API built using FastAPI. It uses an SQLite database (managed by SQLAlchemy) to store audio metadata (title, tags) and extracted acoustic features (tempo, spectral centroid, RMS, duration, ZCR, rolloff). Audio files are uploaded via a POST endpoint and stored locally on the filesystem. Upon upload, librosa is used to extract features. The API provides endpoints for similarity search against an existing audio ID (using Euclidean or Cosine distance on normalized feature vectors), search by feature ranges, text search by title or tags, and a mood-based natural language search that categorizes audio based on feature thresholds.
features: Audio file upload and local storage (supports .wav, .mp3)
Extraction of core audio features (tempo, spectral centroid, RMS, duration, zero-crossing rate, spectral rolloff) using librosa
Storage of extracted features and metadata in an SQLite database
Similarity search between audio tracks based on features (cosine or Euclidean distance)
Search by specified feature ranges (e.g., tempo, RMS)
Text search by audio title or tags
Mood-based natural language search by mapping audio features to descriptive labels
Normalization of feature vectors before similarity computation
Collision-safe file saving for uploaded audio files
Result limiting to top 5 for similarity searches
tradeoffs: Feature extraction relies on basic librosa features; advanced techniques like pre-trained embeddings (e.g., PANNs, OpenL3, MusiCNN) are explicitly not used, limiting the richness of audio representation.
Mood inference is based on simple thresholding of a few features, which may not capture complex musical emotions accurately.
Audio files and metadata are stored locally in a SQLite database and filesystem, making the solution less scalable for large-scale, distributed deployments.
Similarity search loads all audio data into memory for processing, which can become a performance bottleneck with very large datasets.
Text search employs a naive ranking strategy, which may not yield optimal relevance for complex queries.
projects.demonstrates: This project demonstrates the development of a RESTful API using FastAPI, integration of audio processing libraries like librosa for feature extraction, database management with SQLAlchemy and SQLite, implementation of similarity search algorithms (cosine, Euclidean distance) with feature normalization, handling file uploads, and a basic approach to natural language-based audio search using feature-to-label mapping. It showcases modular project structure and dependency management for a Python web service.

projects.name: Social-Network-Friend-Recommendation-System
projects.tagline: A Java project that simulates a friend suggestion engine using graph data structures and algorithms, with a console and Swing GUI.
projects.problem: The project solves the problem of recommending new friends to users based on mutual connections in a social network, allowing for user blocking, and identifying distinct friend communities (circles).
projects.architecture: The system is composed of three main logical units: `SocialGraph` which manages user data, friendships, and blocking relationships using adjacency lists and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for friend circles; `RecommendationEngine` which provides friend recommendations using Breadth-First Search (BFS) and leverages the `SocialGraph`; and a user interface layer provided by `Main.java` (console-based) and `UI.java` (Swing GUI-based) to interact with the core logic.
features: Add Users
Add Friendships (Undirected Graph)
Show All Users
Recommend Friends based on mutual connections (up to 2 levels)
Show Mutual Friends (Names & Count)
Exclude Blocked Users from suggestions
Block Users (bidirectional blocking for suggestions)
Detect Friend Circles (using DSU)
View Social Graph (adjacency list representation)
Console Interface
GUI Interface with Swing (with enhanced styling)
Case-insensitive Input Handling
Sorted Suggestions (by number of mutual friends, then alphabetically)
projects.demonstrates: This project demonstrates the practical application of core graph data structures (adjacency lists) and algorithms (Breadth-First Search, Disjoint Set Union with path compression) to solve a real-world problem like friend recommendation and community detection in a social network. It also showcases fundamental Java programming concepts, object-oriented design, and the development of both console-based and graphical user interfaces (Swing).

projects.name: PatientRecordSystem
projects.tagline: A Spring Boot application for managing patient records, medical histories, and appointments.
projects.problem: Streamlining the process of creating, updating, retrieving, and deleting patient information, medical histories, and appointments within a secure system.
projects.architecture: A RESTful API built with Spring Boot, following a layered architecture (Controllers, Services, Repositories, Models). It uses Spring Data JPA for persistence, Spring Security with JWT for authentication, and global exception handling for error management.
features: Patient Profile Management (Create, retrieve, delete patient details: name, email, contact number, date of birth)
Medical History Management (Add, retrieve, delete entries for patients including history ID, patient ID, disease name, treatment details, and date of diagnosis)
Appointment Management (Retrieve all appointments, list all appointments for a specific patient, update, and delete appointments)
JSON Web Token (JWT) based authentication and authorization
Global exception handling with custom exceptions (e.g., PatientNotFound, AppointmentNotFound, MedicalHistoryInvalid)
projects.demonstrates: Demonstrates building a secure RESTful API using Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA for data access, Spring Security for JWT-based authentication, and structured error handling. It showcases a typical CRUD application for managing entities like Patients, Medical Histories, and Appointments.

projects.name: Book-Finder
projects.tagline: A web application for searching and displaying details about books using the Open Library API.
projects.problem: Enables users to discover books by title and view their corresponding details like description, authors, and publication information.
projects.architecture: The application is a single-page application (SPA) built with React. It uses React Router for declarative navigation. Global state for search terms, book lists, and loading status is managed via React Context API. Data is fetched asynchronously from the Open Library API. The UI is composed of functional components for search forms, book listings, and detailed book views.
features: Search for books by title
Display a list of book search results (up to 20 items per search)
View detailed information for individual books
Loading indicators during data fetching
Search input debouncing
Real-time search suggestions
Responsive design for various screen sizes
projects.demonstrates: Core React concepts, including component architecture, state management with Hooks (`useState`, `useEffect`, `useContext`, `useRef`, `useCallback`), and prop drilling avoidance with Context. Integration with a third-party RESTful API (Open Library) for dynamic content. Client-side routing implementation using `react-router-dom` for a multi-page feel in a SPA. Strategies for handling asynchronous operations and displaying loading states. User input handling, form submission, and optimizing API calls with debouncing. Modular CSS styling and responsive design considerations.

projects.name: Contact-Manager-App
projects.tagline: An Express.js backend API for managing user contacts.
projects.problem: Provides a RESTful API to store, retrieve, update, and delete contact information, secured with user authentication and authorization.
projects.architecture: A Node.js Express application following a modular architecture with separate routes, controllers, models, and middleware. It uses MongoDB for data persistence, JWT for authentication, and bcrypt for password hashing. It includes global error handling.
features: User registration and login.
JWT-based authentication for protecting API routes.
CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) for contacts.
Contacts are associated with individual users.
Custom error handling middleware.
API endpoints for managing users and contacts.
tradeoffs: JWT access tokens have a short expiration (15 minutes), implying a need for a refresh token mechanism not present in the provided code.
Error responses expose stack traces, which could be a security concern in a production environment.
Basic input validation is implemented, but the `express-validator` library is listed as a dependency without apparent usage in the provided controller snippets for more advanced validation.
projects.demonstrates: How to build a RESTful API with Node.js and Express.js, implement user authentication and authorization with JWT and bcrypt, integrate with MongoDB using Mongoose, and structure a backend application with middleware and error handling.
